search_intent: Commercial-investigational. The searcher wants a breathing app they can use without paying and needs to know which "free" apps are really usable for free, which techniques each offers, and whether they even need an app. A neutral, dated roundup with the same fields for every app fits best.
serp_summary: Page one is mostly AppsHunter topic pages (machine-made lists with nothing on free tiers) and three brand roundups (Breethe, Othership, Art of Living). Each brand roundup ranks its own app first without clear disclosure. None dates its prices, and they use "free" loosely to mean a free download with a trial wall. They skip whether you need an account, which techniques each app offers, and built-in options like Apple Watch Mindfulness. None has an honest evidence section or a safety note on breath holds. Art of Living's prices contradict each other, and Othership mixes general meditation apps into its list. What they do well: short entries for each app and "best for" labels.

outline.h2: Is breath holding safe? A short safety note
points: Stop if you feel dizzy or lightheaded and return to normal breathing; practise sitting or lying down, never while driving or in water (general guidance, no citation)
Breath holds and fast breathing are not for everyone: the Stanford trial excluded pregnancy, heart disease, glaucoma, seizure history and more
If the counts make you strain, shorten them, or skip holds and use slow 4-in/6-out breathing
Fast breathwork brought some side effects (hot flushes, shortness of breath, sweating); 10% of Balban participants reported a negative experience
For persistent anxiety, sleep problems or distress, see a professional; in crisis, call 988 (US) or local emergency services

research_notes:
# Research notes: "best free breathing apps"

**Facts checked:** 3 November 2026, US App Store unless noted. Prices are in USD as the listings show them.

## SERP ANALYSIS

**What ranks:**
- **App-directory pages.** About ten AppsHunter "topic" pages show up (free breathing app, free box breathing, free deep breathing, and so on). They are machine-made lists with almost nothing on what the free tier includes.
- **Roundups published by brands.** All three main ones rank their own app first, and none of them clearly discloses that.
  - **Breethe**, "Which free breathing app is best?" (Oct 2025). Compares Breethe, Breathwrk, iBreathe and The Breathing App, in that order. Breethe is named in the title and gets the most space. Its CTA says "Start Your Free Trial" even though it calls Breethe free "as long as you want," and it never reconciles the two. It gives no dollar prices, no safety caveats and no testing method. The ratings it quotes are unverified.
  - **Othership**, "best deep breathing apps" (Mar 2026). Lists 25 apps with Othership at #1. There is no disclosure, no ranking criteria and no date on the prices. It says almost nothing about safety even though Othership itself sells breath-retention practice. It mixes broad meditation apps (Calm, Headspace, Smiling Mind) into a breathing list.
  - **Art of Living**, "15 Best Breathwork Apps (Tested & Ranked)" (updated Sep 2025). Its own app, Sattva, is #1 and is called "Our flagship app" and "the superior choice." It shows no testing method despite the title. Its numbers contradict each other (Breathwrk is $5.75/mo in the text and $69/yr in the table). It promotes breath-hold challenges with no contraindications and has no medical disclaimer.
- **Low-quality or scraped pages** also appear, for example a mirrored "mega-zone" page on a subdomain.

**What they do well:** short entries for each app, "best for" labels, and a mention of the free tier.

**What they get wrong or leave out:**
- Self-ranking without disclosure.
- No date on prices.
- "Free" used loosely to mean a free download with a trial wall.
- Nothing on whether you need an account.
- No mapping of which techniques each app offers (box, 4-7-8, slow exhale, sigh).
- Built-in options are ignored: none of the main roundups treats Apple Watch Mindfulness/Breathe as a free option.
- No evidence section that is honest about limits, and no safety note on breath holds.

## GAPS AND ANGLE

1. **Sort by what you actually get free, using three tiers:**
   - **Truly free:** Apple Mindfulness/Breathe.
   - **Free core that is genuinely usable:** The Breathing App (the listing says "Free forever" for its core features, "No account required," "No ads"), and iBreathe (free with ads, one-time IAPs).
   - **Free download behind a subscription wall:** Calm ("some of the programs and features are free forever") and Breathwrk (the listing does not say what is free).
2. **Use the same fields for every app,** with facts taken only from the listings: free tier, what is paywalled, techniques, account, platforms, price as listed with the check date.
3. **"Do you need an app at all?"** Balban 2023 used just 5 minutes a day of simple protocols, and in the Fincham meta-analysis slow-paced breathing (10 studies) did as well as anything else. A plain pacer is enough, so the article can point to the /tools/ browser timers (box, 4-7-8, calm 4-6, physiological sigh, custom). Use the exact URLs from the site inventory.
4. **Be honest about the evidence.** Effects are small to moderate, the trials carry moderate risk of bias, and in Balban there was no HRV change and only 4 weeks of follow-up. Top results don't do this.
5. **Disclosure and neutrality.** This is a differentiator, because every brand roundup on page one ranks itself.
6. **"Where DeRot fits (our app)."** DeRot is pre-launch. It meets you mid-scroll, so you don't have to remember to open a separate app. It is not for people who want a full meditation library or a hard lockout.
7. **Drop Prana Breath.** Its iOS listing (id6478402874) returned 404 on the US, TH and JP storefronts, so I couldn't verify anything from an official source. Mention it only if the writer can verify it. The same goes for Breethe, Sattva, Breathe+ and Medito: I did not open their official listings, so leave them out or verify them first.
8. **Secondary keywords** map to three subsections: Apple Watch Breathe alternatives, a free Calm alternative, and a free Breathwrk alternative.

## QUESTIONS (People Also Ask style)

I found no Reddit threads. These come from SERP patterns and Product Hunt developer notes, which describe people looking for a simple app "that didn't want a subscription or an account."

- Is there a breathing app that's completely free, with no subscription?
- Is the Apple Watch Breathe app still available? Where did it go? (It is now inside the Mindfulness app.)
- Can I use Apple's Breathe on iPhone without a Watch? (Unclear; see the Apple Mindfulness source note.)
- Is Calm free? What do you get without Premium?
- Is Breathwrk free? Is it owned by Peloton?
- What's the best free app for box breathing or 4-7-8?
- Do I need an app to do breathing exercises?
- How many minutes a day of breathing exercise actually helps?
- Are breathing apps safe? Is breath holding bad for you?

## SOURCES

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9873947/ | Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal | Cell Reports Medicine (Yilmaz Balban, Spiegel, Huberman et al.), via PMC | 2023 |
- **Design:** remote RCT, 108 enrolled. 24 did mindfulness and 84 did breathwork (30 cyclic sighing, 21 box, 33 cyclic hyperventilation with retention). 5 min/day for 28 days. Average days completed: 19.61 (breathwork) and 17.71 (mindfulness).
- **Positive affect:** breathwork overall +1.91 (p<0.0001) vs mindfulness +1.22 (p=0.06). In the mixed model, only cyclic sighing differed significantly from mindfulness, and the effect grew with adherence.
- **Respiratory rate:** breathwork reduced it more than mindfulness (p<0.05). Of the individual groups, only sighing differed significantly. The change correlated with positive affect (r = −0.24).
- **Anxiety:** state anxiety fell in all groups, with no differences between groups. Trait anxiety did not change.
- **Null results:** no significant change in HRV or resting heart rate, and no sleep changes.
- **Limitations:** exploratory, registered retrospectively, adherence self-reported, 4-week follow-up, comparisons among the breathwork groups underpowered.
- **Conflict of interest:** Huberman advises WHOOP, the wearable used in the study.
- **Exclusions:** heart disease, glaucoma, seizure history, pregnancy, psychosis, suicidality, bipolar disorder, substance use disorders.
- **Adverse experiences:** none reported as adverse events, but 10% reported a negative experience in the debrief.
- **Box breathing instruction:** shorten the counts if straining.

https://hubermanlab.stanford.edu/publications/brief-structured-respiration-practices-enhance-mood-and-reduce-physiological-arousal?.com | Brief structured respiration practices… | Stanford (Huberman Lab) | 2023 |
- University publication page for the same trial. It can serve as the "Stanford" attribution link.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9828383/ | Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: a meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials | Scientific Reports (Fincham et al.), via PMC | 2023 |
- **Stress:** 12 RCTs, 785 adults, g = −0.35 (95% CI −0.55 to −0.14), p=0.0009.
- **Anxiety:** 20 RCTs, g = −0.32 (−0.48 to −0.16).
- **Depression:** 18 RCTs, g = −0.40 (−0.58 to −0.22).
- **Slow vs fast breathing:** slow-paced (10 studies) g = −0.35 (−0.61 to −0.10). Fast-paced (2 studies) g = −0.31, CI crossed zero. Two fast studies were too few for a meaningful comparison.
- **Delivery:** remote and self-guided delivery worked about as well as in-person.
- **Limitations:** most studies had moderate risk of bias, there were no physiological outcomes, and follow-up could not be analysed. The authors warn against hype.
- **Safety:** no adverse events were attributed to breathwork. In one fast-paced study, some participants reported hot flushes, shortness of breath or sweating. The authors call for more safety research on fast breathwork.

- Duration: "You can choose a time between 1 and 5 minutes."
- Breath rate is set in Settings > Mindfulness > Breath Rate.
- Haptics can be set to None, Minimal or Prominent.
- Heart rate shows on the Summary screen after a session and is viewable in Health.

- SERP competitor. Brand-published with no explicit disclosure, no prices, no safety notes. (Use for SERP analysis only; do not cite in the article.)

https://www.othership.us/resources/best-deep-breathing-apps | Best deep breathing apps | Othership | 2026 |

**Authority gap:** I found only two primary research sources (Balban 2023 and Fincham 2023) plus Apple's official support page. No university or clinic page on slow-exhale breathing or HRV, and no government safety guidance, came up in my 10 searches. Before publishing, add one authoritative clinic or government page on breathing exercises or safety. Without it, keep the physiology claims to what these two papers support.

## SAFETY

- **Breath holds and fast breathing.** Balban's trial excluded people with heart disease, glaucoma, seizure history, pregnancy, psychosis, bipolar disorder, suicidality and substance use disorders. Readers in those groups should skip breath holds and hyperventilation styles (box holds, 4-7-8 holds, "breath-hold challenges") or check with a clinician first. Present this as general caution, not a clinical rule.
- **Strain.** Balban's box protocol tells people to shorten the counts if they have to strain. Recommend the same: shorter holds or no holds (slow 4-in/6-out instead).
- **Stop if dizzy or lightheaded**, then return to normal breathing. Practice sitting or lying down, never while driving or in water. (I found this only in non-authoritative sources, so state it as general DeRot guidance without a citation.)
- **Fast breathwork side effects.** In Fincham's review, some people doing fast breathwork reported hot flushes, shortness of breath or sweating, and the authors call for more safety data. In Balban, 10% reported a negative experience.
- **No overclaiming.** Effects are small to moderate, the studies carry moderate risk of bias, and Balban found no HRV change. Don't say breathing "treats" anxiety or insomnia. Apps are not a substitute for care: point readers with persistent anxiety, sleep problems or distress to a professional, and anyone in crisis to 988 (US) or local emergency services.
- **App caveats for readers.** Several apps auto-renew after a trial (the Calm listing describes auto-renew). Tell readers to check trial terms before tapping "start trial."
